Does wet brining help remove undesirable flavors from chicken?

There are various techniques intended to remove blood and other impurities from meat to produce a cleaner flavor - e.g. soaking meat in cold water before making soup or blanching meat and bones before making stock. I'm wondering whether wet brining has a similar benefit, particularly for chicken.

 My goal is to make roasted or pan-seared chicken with the cleanest possible chicken flavor. I'm considering wet brining the chicken, then letting it air-dry uncovered overnight in the fridge before cooking so I can still get a good amount of browning.

 I don't know which recipe is the best, and afraid to ruin it on my first try. Maybe I'm overthinking this (because each family and person has their own way of making the dish), but I wouldn't like to throw it away or leave it in the fridge until it spoils.

 ___

 UPDATE: I went an easy route and liked the result, so here is my version.

 Ingredients:

 - 800 ml water

 - 200 g dry pasta (preferably macaroni)

 - 200 g mature cheddar cheese + 50 g vintage cheddar cheese (alternatively, 1:1)

 - 50 g butter

 - Spices to taste (salt, ground black pepper, smoked paprika, chili/cayenne pepper, garlic powder)

 ___

 Preparation:

  - Bring water to a boil in a pot

 - Add some salt and dissolve it in the water, then put in your pasta of choice

 - While you're waiting for pasta, grate the cheese and mix two types of cheddar together; set aside 50 grams

 - Boil the pasta until halfway done (about 5 minutes), then poor out extra liquid until the water barely covers the pasta

 - Reduce the heat, add some milk and bring to a boil again (be careful so it doesn't spill over the edge!) If it seems like there's too much liquid, it's only for now; it will evaporate and thicken quickly

 - Add some butter and let it dissolve

 - Add the rest of your spices to the pasta and mix well

 - Add grated cheese to the pasta; mix until it melts

 - Set the oven to grill mode; pour the pasta into a baking dish with some cheese on top (the 50 grams we set aside earlier)

 - Put the baking dish into the oven; wait for 5 minutes

 - Serve Mac 'n' Cheese with herbs of choice (you can use a cake server), or eat just like this

Follow-up on cutting gumdrops

I posted a couple days ago asking for tips on cutting up gumdrops for a fruitcake. I got tons of tips so thank you all for that. I made the cake this morning and tried a bunch of the suggestions. I thought I'd report back on what worked and what didn't.

 Kitchen scissors didn't work well. Mine have fairly thick blades so it was difficult to cut through the gumdrops and they collected a lot of goo. Putting flour, powdered sugar, and oil on the blades didn't make a big difference.

 Using my mini-chopper didn't work at all. When I tried just a handful of gumdrops it didn't cut them at all, just bounced them around the bowl. When I filled it about half full the blades got bound up and stopped spinning.

 I tried a gift card, it couldn't cut them at all.

 I tried a wire cheese slicer, it also couldn't cut them at all. 

 A serrated knife didn't help much. The issue isn't cutting through them so much as them not separating off the blade easily afterward.

 I tried wetting the knife blade and heating it in the past and those didn't help at all.

 The main tip that I didn't end up trying was freezing the gumdrops or chilling them first, because I was busy last night and forgot to put them in the fridge/freezer.

 What ended up working best was using the thinnest-bladed knife I own (a Wusthof 8" slicing knife). I sprayed Pam on a paper towel and rubbed it on the blade before cutting. About every 20 gumdrops I used hot water to rinse the goo off the knife blade and re-coated it with Pam. After that I tossed them in a bowl with a half cup of the flour for the cake to keep them from glomming back together. It was still a pain in the ass but less so than in past years.

The best (and easiest) beer brats of all time

It’s simple. Get a pot. Dice a couple white onions. Throw them in the pot. Add a bunch of butter, onion powder, garlic powder, a fuck ton of smoked paprika, and a bit of cayenne. Eyeball just enough high life so that when you add the brats they will be just submerged (less is better). Bring this to a gentle boil directly on the grill and give them a little head start. 

 Then give your brats a nice char on the other side of the grill, rotating frequently until they look like a brat you’d see on a commercial. Once they look dynamite set them in the beer bath to simmer on low for 30 minutes. They’ll stay delicious like this for hours, just be careful not to boil them. I eat mine on a bun with some secret stadium sauce and some of those delicious onions from the broth. 

 This is the easiest game day meal of all time and it’s so so good. The broth ends up smelling like onions and garlic bread. The brats end up perfectly cooked and stay juicy for hours, and the onions just soak up that broth which is not only delicious in its own right but ends up flavored with the fat and juices from the sausage. It’s a perfect dish.

Amaranth and Honey Skulls from "Dining With the Dead"

- Makes 2 large amaranth skulls

  Ingredients

  - ¼ cup water

 - 150 grams piloncillo sugar, grated

 - ½ cup honey

 - 1 teaspoon lime juice

 - 16 ounces puffed amaranth

 - 2 pinches ground cinnamon 

 - Royal icing, seeds, and dried fruit, for decorating

 - 1 or 2 large skull molds\*

  Instructions

  - In a small pot, heat up the water and piloncillo and stir until the piloncillo dissolves. Add the honey and lime juice, and bring to a low simmer. Stir constantly until half the liquid has evaporated and it has the consistency of honey. Remove from the heat and let the syrup cool down, for two to three minutes. 

 - Add the puffed amaranth and gently stir using a wood spatula. Once the amaranth is cool enough to handle, rub your hands with some cooking oil and gently knead the mixture until the syrup is evenly distributed. 

 - Promptly fill two skull molds (see note below) and press down to get a solid skull. If the mixture is too sticky, add more oil to your hands. Level and even out the back of each skull. Place a piece of cardboard behind the mold and flip it over. To help release the mold, tap on the skull, forehead, and chin. Let the skull dry for about 24 hours. The next day, carefully glue the two skull halves together using the royal icing. 

 - At this point, your skull is still fragile but dry enough on the outside to decorate. Use royal icing to glue seeds onto the face. Mariana McEnroe uses pepitas around the eyes, prunes for the eye cavity, roasted peanuts for the forehead and teeth, two almond halves for the nose, and pecans for the top of the skull. 

 - These skulls are edible within two to three days, and good to display for more than a month.

Well, it would seem the secret to perfect rice is a good soak and remembering the differences in volume measurements…

Reading through every “perfect rice” method inevitably comes to rice/water ratios, with many of these methods quite divergent, going as far out as 2:1 water to rice, all of which I can say I have tried with inconsistent success and failure.

 Where I found the most success has been at a 1:1 ratio, while the struggle had remained in consistent results from a consistent method.

 Turns out where the most failure I had was accidentally discovered adjacent to washing my rice, but not so simply that “washing rice produced consistent results” was the aha moment as much as what I learned when washing was part of the answer.

 Being pretty insistent on washing rice extendedly, the thought never occurred to me how much water the rice was absorbing depending on how I washed it, meaning, washing and rinsing rice quickly absorbed less water than washing and rinsing rice deep in a water bath.

 That absorption directly affects how much water will be needed in the pot with when cooking, which one would think affects the ratio, but I’ve learned it doesn’t, or rather, it requires an understanding of ratios using solid and liquid volume measures as your guide.

 What I learned using a 1:1 ratio is that adding these measures together does not produce an equivalent liquid volume, which really pisses me off since I never realized this until I actually measured it out using a 3/4 solid measure cup of rice (which is the measure of a rice cooker cup) with 3/4 liquid measure cup of water, producing 1.25cups liquid measure when combined.

 Why this is important is that when washing and soaking the rice, what is needed when ready to cook will STILL be 1.25 cups, which again made me feel really stupid not thinking about this before, while a good soak guarantees the center of the grain will come to temperature at the same rate as the rest of the grain.

 Especially when soaking the rice for an extended period of time, it’s gonna look weird because it looks like too little water, but thinking about how much water has been absorbed, more water past the original volume measurement produces an exponential rate of overhydrating the rice.

 All that remained was remembering how a rice cooker uses some pretty low amounts of heat to gently get the water JUST to boiling point and a nice pot with a good fitting lid, and this measurement has produced perfectly consistent rice for quite some time.

 My final formalization of this method will be to use weight measures vs volume measures, as I believe this, along with consistent washing and soaking methods, will yield a perfect recipe.
